```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 110)
```

Today we read a PCA instead of running one. You get the **output** of a principal components
analysis of ~1,000 West Eurasian and ~300 East Eurasian individuals, part of it ancient DNA, and
your job is to work out what the plot is telling you about European and Siberian population history.

The West Eurasian analysis recreates the PCA in
[Mathieson et al. (2015), *Nature* 528:499–503](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16152),
*Genome-wide patterns of selection in 230 ancient Eurasians*. You don't have to read the paper, but
we will compare our plot to the one in its Figure 1.

**By the end of this document you should be able to:**

1. Explain what each number in the data file is: what one row, one `PC` column and one point in the
   plot represent.
2. Explain what *projection* means and why ancient samples are projected onto modern variation
   rather than used to compute the axes.
3. Read a PCA plot: what the axes mean, what they *don't* mean, and why in this dataset you
   **cannot** judge a PC's importance from how wide the cloud looks.
4. Say which real population-genetic processes put the West Eurasian clusters where they are.
5. Judge for yourself when a higher PC still carries population signal and when it is just noise.
6. Spot a data error by plotting before testing — this dataset contains some.

> **This is the solved version**: every exercise is already filled in, so you can run or knit the
> whole file and concentrate on the interpretation. The answers to the hand-in questions are not in
> here — those are yours to write.
>
> The version with the exercises left open is [`pca_eurasia.Rmd`](pca_eurasia.Rmd).

Sections 1–5 build the ideas; Sections 6–10 are the hand-in questions.

<details>
<summary><b>📦 R refresher: the base-R syntax used here (open if you're rusty)</b></summary>

```r
nrow(df); ncol(df); dim(df)       # size of a data frame
head(df)                          # first 6 rows
names(df)                         # the column names
str(df)                           # structure: column types and first few values
df$PC1                            # one column, as a vector
df[, c("PC1", "PC2")]             # two columns, as a data frame

subset(df, POP == "Finnish")           # keep rows where POP is exactly "Finnish"
subset(df, POP %in% c("Finnish", "Czech"))   # ... one of several values

aggregate(PC1 ~ POP, data = df, FUN = mean)            # mean of PC1 per population
aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ POP, data = df, FUN = mean)  # several columns at once
tapply(df$PC1, df$POP, mean)      # the same thing, as a named vector
```

```{r helpers}
# Round only the numeric columns of a data frame. `round()` alone fails on a table that
# also has a text column, which is what `aggregate()` hands back.
round_num <- function(df, digits = 4) {
  is_num <- vapply(df, is.numeric, logical(1))
  df[is_num] <- round(df[is_num], digits)
  df
}
```

## 0.2 Getting the data

The three data files are plain tab-separated text, ~140 kB in total. The chunk below looks for them
in a `data/` folder next to this file or one folder up (where they live in the course repository),
and downloads them from GitHub if it can't find them. You don't need to change anything here.

```{r data}
data_files <- c("dataWE.txt", "dataEE.txt", "dataWE_LatLong.txt")
repo_raw <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emmadiepeveen/Evolutionary_Thinking_2026/main/week47/Friday/"

find_or_download_data <- function() {
  for (folder in c("data", "../data", ".")) {
    if (all(file.exists(file.path(folder, data_files)))) {
      cat("Found the data in:", normalizePath(folder), "\n")
      return(folder)
    }
  }

  cat("Data not found locally - downloading (~140 kB)...\n")
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  for (name in data_files) {
    ok <- tryCatch({
      download.file(paste0(repo_raw, "data/", name), file.path("data", name), quiet = TRUE)
      TRUE
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (!ok) {
      # fall back to the zipped copies one level up in the repository
      tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
      download.file(paste0(repo_raw, name, ".zip"), tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
      unzip(tmp, files = name, exdir = "data", junkpaths = TRUE)
    }
    cat("  downloaded", name, "\n")
  }
  "data"
}

data_dir <- find_or_download_data()
```

# 1. What a PCA actually did to these data

You met PCA in week 44 on goat genotypes. Here is the same idea in four sentences, because
everything in this document depends on it.

**Start from the genotype matrix.** Every individual was genotyped at hundreds of thousands of
**SNPs** (positions in the genome where people differ by a single DNA letter). At each SNP you store
how many copies of one chosen allele the individual carries: `0`, `1` or `2`. So each individual is
one row of a huge table of 0s, 1s and 2s.

**That makes each individual a point in a space with one dimension per SNP.** With 500,000 SNPs,
each person is a point in 500,000-dimensional space. Two people with similar genomes sit close
together in that space, because they have similar genotypes at most SNPs.

**PCA finds the directions in which that cloud of points is most stretched out.** The direction of
greatest spread is **PC1**. The direction of greatest remaining spread, at right angles to PC1, is
**PC2**, then PC3, and so on. These directions are combinations of all the SNPs at once, not single
SNPs.

**The `PC1` and `PC2` columns in your data file are where each individual falls along those
directions.** Projecting a 500,000-dimensional cloud onto its two most-stretched directions is the
most informative flat picture of it you can draw — like choosing the angle to photograph a sculpture
from so you lose as little of its shape as possible.

The important consequence: **the axes have no units and no intrinsic meaning.** Nobody designed PC1
to be "north–south" or "farmer ancestry". It came out of the data as "the direction along which
these particular individuals differ most". What it *means* is something you work out afterwards, by
looking at which populations sit at its ends. We will do exactly that in Section 4.

### ❓ Question: Check your understanding

1. Two individuals end up at almost the same point in the PC1–PC2 plot. What does that tell you?
2. The sign of a PC is arbitrary: software could return `PC1` or `-PC1` and both are equally
   correct. What does that mean for how you describe a plot?
3. Suppose you add 200 more Finnish individuals to the dataset and re-run the PCA. Could the axes
   change?

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal answer</b></summary>

1. It tells you their genotypes are similar **in the directions PC1 and PC2 describe** — usually
      read as "similar genome-wide ancestry". It does **not** necessarily mean that they are closely
   related, or that they come from the same place, or that they are similar in the directions
   PC3, PC4, … describe.
2. Say "Population A and B sit at **opposite ends** of PC1", not "A has a high PC1". If you re-ran
   the analysis the plot might come out mirrored, and that would mean nothing. Only relative
   positions carry information.
3. Yes. PCA finds the directions of greatest spread **in the sample you give it**.
   Over-representing one population makes the differences involving that population a bigger share
   of the total    spread, so an axis can rotate towards it.

</details>

# 2. Where these numbers came from, and why you're not computing them

## 2.1 smartPCA

The analysis was run with `smartPCA` from the [Eigensoft](https://github.com/DReichLab/EIG)
package, the standard tool for this in human population genetics.
We are **not** running it today — it needs the full genotype data.

`smartPCA` reads a parameter file pointing at four inputs:

| Input | Contents |
|---|---|
| `.geno` | The genotype matrix: individuals left to right, SNPs top to bottom. |
| `.snp` | One line per SNP: name, chromosome, genetic position, physical position, reference allele, alternative allele. |
| `.ind` | One line per individual: individual name, sex (`M`/`F`/`U`), population name. |
| *population list* | **The list of populations whose individuals are used to compute the PCs.** |


## 2.2 The population list, and projection

Why not compute the axes from everybody?

**First off:** there are too many individuals and the computation gets slow.

**But the real reason:** Ancient samples have systematic problems that modern samples don't:

* **Low coverage and lots of missing data.** Each ancient genome is sequenced shallowly, so many
  genotypes are missing or uncertain, and the pattern of missingness differs between samples.
* **Post-mortem damage.** Cytosine deaminates to uracil over time, which is read as a C→T change
  (and G→A on the other strand). Older or worse-preserved samples carry more of these errors.
* **Contamination** with modern human DNA from excavators and lab staff, and with environmental
  microbial DNA.
* **Reference bias.** Short, damaged reads map more readily to the reference allele, so
  heterozygotes get under-called, and the direction of the error depends on read length.
* **Batch effects.** Different labs, extraction protocols, capture panels and sequencing runs leave
  their own fingerprints.

Here is the problem: these artefacts are **shared by samples processed similarly** and **not shared
with modern samples**. They are a large, consistent source of variation. PCA finds the directions of
greatest variation — so if you let ancient samples define the axes, a leading PC can easily end up
describing *sequencing batch* or *how degraded the sample is* rather than ancestry. You would get a
beautiful plot of your laboratory's history.

**The fix is projection.** The PCs are computed from the modern populations in the population list
only. Then **every** individual, ancient ones included, is placed on those already-fixed axes by
taking their genotypes and working out where they fall along each direction. The ancient samples get
coordinates in the plot without having had any say in where the axes point.

This is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch. Ancient populations may carry variation that no
modern population has, and projection is blind to it by construction: an axis that was never drawn
cannot show you anything. Projection also **shrinks** projected points towards the origin — the more
missing data a sample has, the more it shrinks — so an ancient individual sitting between two modern
clusters is not automatically admixed between them. In practice, avoiding the artefacts is worth
more than the lost variation, and the approach breaks down only once the samples get so old and so
distant from modern variation that the modern axes are no longer informative about them.

# 3. The West Eurasian data

## 3.1 Reading the file

`dataWE.txt` is tab-separated with a header line.

```{r read-we}
dataWE <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "dataWE.txt"), sep = "\t", header = TRUE)

cat("rows (individuals), columns:", dim(dataWE), "\n")
head(dataWE)
```

Each **row is one individual**. The columns are:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `IND` | The individual's ID. Modern individuals have IDs like `abh24.HO`; ancient ones like `RISE507` or `I0061`. |
| `PC1` … `PC10` | Where that individual falls along each of the first ten principal components. |
| `POP` | The population the individual is assigned to. |
| `ModAnc` | A grouping of the populations — see below, it is not what you'd expect. |

Work out:

1. how many individuals there are in total (`n_individuals`),
2. how many different populations (`n_populations`),
3. which populations have the most individuals (show the top 10).

* `length(unique(df$col))` counts how many *different* values a column has.

```{r solved-feel}
n_individuals <- nrow(dataWE)
n_populations <- length(unique(dataWE$POP))

cat("Individuals:", n_individuals, "\n")
cat("Populations:", n_populations, "\n")

head(sort(table(dataWE$POP), decreasing = TRUE), 10)
```

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal solution</b></summary>

```r
n_individuals <- nrow(dataWE)
n_populations <- length(unique(dataWE$POP))

cat("Individuals:", n_individuals, "\n")
cat("Populations:", n_populations, "\n")

head(sort(table(dataWE$POP), decreasing = TRUE), 10)
```

997 individuals in 89 populations. The largest are `Turkish` (56), `Spanish` (53), `Druze` (39) and
`Palestinian` (38) — and note that the fifth largest, `Central_LNBA` (35), is an *ancient* group.

Look at the tail, though: the **median population has only 9 individuals**, 72 of the 89 have fewer
than 15, and 50 have fewer than 10. Two consequences worth carrying with you:

* A cluster of four points is four people. Don't read much into exactly where it sits.
* The populations are very unevenly sampled, and Section 1 told you that over-representing a
  population pulls the axes towards it. 56 Turkish and 53 Spanish individuals have more say in where
  PC1 points than 7 Finnish ones do.

</details>

## 3.2 The `ModAnc` column

```{r modanc}
table(dataWE$ModAnc)
```

They are **archaeological/ancestry groupings**:

| `ModAnc` | Who | Roughly when |
|---|---|---|
| `Modern` | Present-day West Eurasians. **These are the individuals the PCs were computed from.** Everything else is projected. | today |
| `Hunter-gatherer` | Western and Scandinavian Mesolithic hunter-gatherers (`WHG`, `Motala_HG`) | ~9,000–5,000 BCE |
| `EHG` | **E**astern European **h**unter-**g**atherers, from Karelia and the Samara region | ~8,000–5,000 BCE |
| `Early-farmer` | Neolithic farmers of Anatolian origin and their European descendants (`Anatolia_Neolithic`, `LBK_EN`, `Iberia_EN`/`MN`, `Hungary_EN`, `Central_MN`, `Remedello`, `Iberia_Chalcolithic`, and the Iceman) | ~7,000–2,500 BCE |
| `Steppe` | Bronze Age pastoralists of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (`Yamnaya`, `Afanasievo`, `Poltavka`, `Sintashta`, `Andronovo`, `Srubnaya`) **and** the later central/northern European groups that carry steppe ancestry (`Central_LNBA` ≈ Corded Ware, `Bell_Beaker_LN`, `Northern_LNBA`, `Hungary_BA`) | ~3,300–1,000 BCE |
| `Samara_Eneolithic` | Two Copper Age individuals from the Samara region, left as their own category | ~5,000–4,000 BCE |

Let's see how the populations sit inside these categories.

```{r pops-by-group}
# one row per (ModAnc, POP) combination, with the number of individuals
by_group <- as.data.frame(table(dataWE$ModAnc, dataWE$POP))
names(by_group) <- c("ModAnc", "POP", "n")
by_group <- by_group[by_group$n > 0, ]
by_group[order(by_group$ModAnc, by_group$POP), ]
```

### Two things in this output are data errors, not biology

Look carefully at the population names and you will spot:

**1. Some names are mangled: `Modernaltese`, `Modernordovian`, `Modernotala_HG`.** These are
`Maltese`, `Mordovian` and `Motala_HG`. At some point somebody replaced the letter `M` with the word
`Modern` across the whole file — presumably turning a `ModAnc` column that said `M` into one that
said `Modern` — and the replacement also hit every population name starting with `M`. No other
letter was affected, which is why `Anatolia_Neolithic` survived intact.

**2. `Anatolia_Neolithic` appears in two `ModAnc` groups** (21 individuals as `Early-farmer`, 3 as
`Steppe`), and `Samara_Eneolithic` appears both as its own `ModAnc` and inside `Steppe`. These are
labelling inconsistencies in how the file was assembled. Anatolian Neolithic individuals are early
farmers; the three filed under `Steppe` are mislabelled.

Neither error affects the PC values themselves — the coordinates are fine, only the labels are
wrong. We will fix the names, leave the duplicated `ModAnc` assignment alone (it is three
individuals out of 997), and note it when it matters.

# 4. The headline plot

## 4.1 Helpers for plotting PCs

`.data[[x]]` inside `aes()` is how you tell ggplot "the column whose *name* is in the variable `x`",
rather than a column literally called `x`.

```{r plot-helpers}
plot_pcs <- function(df, x = "PC1", y = "PC2", colour = "POP", title = NULL, size = 1.8) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = .data[[y]], colour = .data[[colour]])) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey88") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey88") +
    geom_point(size = size, alpha = 0.85) +
    labs(x = x, y = y, colour = colour, title = title)
}

# Stack several PC pairs into one long table, so they can be drawn as facets of one plot.
# `pairs` is a list of two-element character vectors, e.g. list(c("PC1","PC2"), c("PC3","PC4")).
pc_pairs_long <- function(df, pairs, colour = "POP") {
  labels <- vapply(pairs, function(p) paste(p[1], "vs", p[2]), character(1))
  stacked <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(p, lab) {
    data.frame(x = df[[p[1]]], y = df[[p[2]]],
               group = df[[colour]], pair = lab)
  }, pairs, labels))
  stacked$pair <- factor(stacked$pair, levels = labels)
  stacked
}

plot_pc_pairs <- function(df, pairs, colour = "POP", title = NULL, free_scales = FALSE) {
  stacked <- pc_pairs_long(df, pairs, colour)
  ggplot(stacked, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = group)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey88") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey88") +
    geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.85) +
    facet_wrap(~ pair, nrow = 1, scales = if (free_scales) "free" else "fixed") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = colour, title = title)
}

cat("plot_pcs, pc_pairs_long and plot_pc_pairs are defined.\n")
```

## 4.3 Reading the plot

You should see a large arc or crescent of `Modern` individuals, with the ancient groups falling
inside and along it. This is the structure in Figure 1 of Mathieson et al. (2015), and the reason it
is such a famous plot is that **the ancient groups land in interpretable places**.

To interpret the axes: look at which populations sit at the ends.
Because the modern individuals define the axes, we look at *their* extremes.

```{r axis-extremes}
PCS <- paste0("PC", 1:10)

modern <- subset(dataWE, ModAnc == "Modern")

# mean of every PC within every modern population
pop_means <- aggregate(modern[, PCS], by = list(POP = modern$POP), FUN = mean)
rownames(pop_means) <- pop_means$POP

describe_axis <- function(pc, n = 5) {
  ordered <- pop_means[order(pop_means[[pc]]), ]
  fmt <- function(rows) paste(sprintf("%s (%+.3f)", rows$POP, rows[[pc]]), collapse = ", ")
  cat(pc, "\n",
      "  one end:   ", fmt(head(ordered, n)), "\n",
      "  other end: ", fmt(tail(ordered, n)), "\n\n", sep = "")
}

for (pc in c("PC1", "PC2")) describe_axis(pc)
```

That gives the axes their meaning:

* **PC1** runs from the **northeast European** populations (Lithuanian, Estonian, Finnish, Russian)
  at one end to the **Arabian peninsula and Near East** (Bedouin, Yemenite Jews, Saudi) at the
  other. It is essentially the southeast–northwest cline of West Eurasian variation.
* **PC2** separates the **Caucasus** (Abkhasian, North Ossetian, Chechen, Georgian, Lezgin) from
  **Sardinians, Basques and Bedouins**. Combined with PC1 this spreads the modern populations into
  the familiar arc, with Europe along one arm and the Near East along the other.

Now the ancient groups:

```{r ancient-means}
ancient <- subset(dataWE, ModAnc != "Modern")

round_num(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ ModAnc, data = ancient, FUN = mean), 4)
table(ancient$ModAnc)
```

Before reading the group means off a table, put them on the plot.

```{r ancient-overview, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# A few modern populations to orient yourself by. Change these if you like.
reference_pops <- c("Sardinian", "Basque", "Spanish", "French", "English", "Norwegian",
                    "Finnish", "Estonian", "Lithuanian", "Russian", "Greek", "Turkish",
                    "Abkhasian", "Druze", "BedouinA", "BedouinB")

ancient_colours <- c("Hunter-gatherer" = "#1f77b4", "EHG" = "#17becf",
                     "Early-farmer" = "#2ca02c", "Steppe" = "#d62728",
                     "Samara_Eneolithic" = "#9467bd")

ancient_means <- aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ ModAnc, data = ancient, FUN = mean)
reference <- pop_means[reference_pops, ]

ggplot() +
  # every modern individual, as a pale backdrop
  geom_point(data = modern, aes(PC1, PC2), colour = "grey88", size = 1.2) +
  # the ancient individuals, faintly
  geom_point(data = ancient, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = ModAnc), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.35) +
  # the modern populations you are orienting by
  geom_label(data = reference, aes(PC1, PC2, label = POP),
             size = 2.6, colour = "grey30", fill = "white", alpha = 0.7,
             linewidth = 0, label.padding = unit(0.08, "lines")) +
  # the ancient GROUP MEANS, which is what the question is about
  geom_point(data = ancient_means, aes(PC1, PC2, fill = ModAnc),
             shape = 23, size = 5, stroke = 0.9, colour = "black") +
  geom_label(data = ancient_means, aes(PC1, PC2, label = ModAnc, colour = ModAnc),
             size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", fill = "white", alpha = 0.9,
             vjust = -0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ancient_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ancient_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "PC1   (northeast Europe \u2190\u2192 Near East)",
       y = "PC2   (Sardinia / Basque / Bedouin \u2190\u2192 Caucasus)",
       title = "Where each ancient group sits (diamonds = group means)",
       subtitle = "grey = modern individuals, pale colour = individual ancient samples")
```

### ❓ Question: What the ancient groups' positions mean

Given that PC1 runs northeast-Europe (negative) to Near-East (positive), and looking at where each
ancient group sits, work out the story. Think about it before revealing.

1. `Hunter-gatherer` and `EHG` sit at the far **negative** end of PC1, beyond every modern
   population. What does "beyond the modern range" tell you?
2. `Early-farmer` sits near PC1 ≈ 0 with a clearly **negative PC2**, close to modern Sardinians.
   Why Sardinians?
3. `Steppe` sits **between** the hunter-gatherers and the early farmers. What is the standard
   interpretation, and what is the caveat from Section 2?
4. Modern northern Europeans sit between all three ancient groups rather than on top of any one of
   them. What does that suggest?

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal answer</b></summary>

1. No present-day population is a direct, unmixed continuation of European Mesolithic
   hunter-gatherers. Every modern European carries substantial later ancestry (farmer, steppe),
   which pulls them away from the hunter-gatherer extreme. That ancestry has not disappeared — it is
   diluted. (Part of the distance is also projection shrinkage and the low coverage of these few
   samples, so don't over-read the exact position of a 3-individual group.)
2. Sardinians are the modern population with the **highest proportion of early-farmer ancestry**,
   because Sardinia received comparatively little of the later steppe-related gene flow that
   reshaped mainland Europe. They are often described as the closest modern proxy for Neolithic
   European farmers — which is why early farmers project right next to them.
3. The standard interpretation is that Bronze Age steppe populations were themselves a mixture, with
   roughly half their ancestry from eastern hunter-gatherers and much of the rest from Caucasus and
   Near-Eastern-related sources — and that their expansion into Europe after ~3000 BCE brought that
   ancestry west. The caveat: *this plot alone* does not establish any of it. An intermediate
   position is consistent with admixture but also with shared drift or with projection shrinkage.
   The admixture conclusion comes from f-statistics and qpAdm in the original papers, not from the
   scatter plot.
4. That modern northern Europeans are **mixtures of all three** ancient sources — hunter-gatherer,
   early farmer and steppe — in varying proportions. This is the central result of the 2015 ancient
   DNA papers: present-day Europeans are not the descendants of one ancient population but of
   several successive waves. Again: the plot makes it visible and plausible; the formal methods make
   it a finding.

</details>

## 4.4 The full map of modern populations

The plot above named sixteen populations to orient you. Here is the same space with **every**
modern population labelled at its mean, and the ancient groups left off so that nothing is hidden
behind them. Read it as a map: the arc really does run from the Baltic, round through central and
southern Europe, to the Levant and the Arabian peninsula. Keep it to hand — Sections 6 and 7 ask
you to interpret small groups of these populations. (Nothing to do here.)

```{r labelled-overview, fig.width=11, fig.height=9}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = modern, aes(PC1, PC2), colour = "grey85", size = 1.1) +
  # check_overlap drops labels that would collide, which keeps the crowded
  # northern-European corner readable
  geom_text(data = pop_means, aes(PC1, PC2, label = POP),
            size = 2.1, colour = "grey35", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "PC1   (northeast Europe \u2190\u2192 Near East)",
       y = "PC2   (Sardinia / Basque / Bedouin \u2190\u2192 Caucasus)",
       title = "A map of modern West Eurasian variation",
       subtitle = "every modern individual in grey, each population labelled at its mean")
```

# 5. Warning

A PCA result normally comes with the **variance explained** by each PC: "PC1 explains 4.2% of the
variance, PC2 1.1%", and so on. That number is how you judge whether a PC is worth looking at, and
it is why PC1 is usually the widest axis on the plot and later PCs are visibly narrower.

**Your data file does not contain those numbers.** `smartPCA` writes the eigenvalues to a separate
output file, and you were only given the coordinates. So you cannot report variance explained for
these PCs — if a question asks you to, say that the eigenvalues weren't provided.

Worse, you cannot sneak up on the answer by looking at how wide each axis is. Here is why.

```{r normalisation}
# For each PC: the sum of squared scores, over the modern individuals only
cat("sum of squared scores, modern individuals:\n")
print(round(colSums(modern[, PCS]^2), 4))

cat("\nstandard deviation, modern individuals:\n")
print(round(apply(modern[, PCS], 2, sd), 4))

cat("\n1 / sqrt(n - 1) with n =", nrow(modern), ":",
    round(1 / sqrt(nrow(modern) - 1), 4), "\n")
```

Every PC has sum of squares **exactly 1**, and therefore exactly the same standard deviation,
0.0359, which is precisely $1/\sqrt{n-1}$ for the 777 modern individuals.

`smartPCA` **normalised every principal component to unit length.** The eigenvalue — the thing that
says how important a PC is — has been divided out of the coordinates and stored elsewhere. So:

> **In this dataset, PC10 occupies exactly as much width on the page as PC1.**
> The spread of the cloud carries **no** information about how much variance a PC explains.


A couple of smaller consequences worth knowing:

* The spread of **all 997** individuals is slightly wider than 0.0359 on PC1–PC4. That is the
  projected ancient individuals, who were not part of the normalisation. On PC5–PC10 it is back to
  0.0318 — the ancients barely budge from the origin on those axes, which is itself a hint about how
  much population signal is left in them.
* The East Eurasian file in Section 9 was **not** normalised the same way (its sums of squares are
  not 1 and differ between PCs), so don't assume the two files are on a common scale. They are
  separate analyses with separate axes; a `PC1` in one has nothing to do with a `PC1` in the other.

```{r normalisation-all}
cat("all 997 individuals, sd per PC:\n")
print(round(apply(dataWE[, PCS], 2, sd), 4))
```

```{r solved-q3}
my_subset <- subset(dataWE, POP %in% my_pops)
print(plot_pcs(my_subset, x = "PC1", y = "PC2", colour = "POP",
               title = paste("PC1 vs PC2:", paste(my_pops, collapse = ", "))))

print(round_num(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ POP, data = my_subset, FUN = mean), 4))
```


**What this particular choice shows.** The four form an ordered gradient along PC1 and PC2 that
matches the map: Italian_North, then Italian_South, then Greek, running towards the eastern
Mediterranean — with Sardinian sitting well off the line at the extreme negative-PC2 end.

Two different processes:

* **The Italy–Greece gradient is isolation by distance plus gene flow.** Neighbouring populations
  exchange migrants, so allele frequencies change gradually with distance instead of in jumps. A
  smooth cline in a PCA plot is the signature of this. Note that a cline means you cannot really
  speak of discrete "populations" here at all — the labels are administrative, the variation is
  continuous.
* **Sardinia's position is isolation plus drift, and retained early-farmer ancestry.** An island
  population with limited immigration keeps more of its Neolithic ancestry and drifts on its own
  trajectory. That is also why early farmers project next to Sardinians in Section 4.

</details>

Plot PC3 against PC4 for the English/Norwegian/Finnish/Icelandic subset. Compare with the PC1–PC2

<details>
<summary><b>💡 Hint (click to open)</b></summary>

Use the `plot_pc_pairs` helper to get both panels in one plot:

```r

```

(`free_scales = TRUE` lets each panel zoom to its own data, which is what you want here because
you are comparing *shapes*. In Section 7.2 you will want `FALSE` instead.)

</details>

```{r solved-q4, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.6}
plot_pc_pairs(nordic, list(c("PC1", "PC2"), c("PC3", "PC4")),
              free_scales = TRUE,
              title = "The same 40 individuals on two different pairs of axes")
```

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal solution</b></summary>

```r
plot_pc_pairs(nordic, list(c("PC1", "PC2"), c("PC3", "PC4")),
              free_scales = TRUE,
              title = "The same 40 individuals on two different pairs of axes")
```

</details>

The plot shows the populations sitting further apart on some axes than others. These are the
numbers behind that: the population means on PC1–PC4, and **Cohen's *d*** for the comparisons that
matter — the distance between two group means in units of their pooled standard deviation.
Roughly, *d* = 1 means the means are one standard deviation apart, and by *d* ≈ 3 the two groups
barely overlap.

```{r cohens-d}
cohens_d <- function(a, b, pc) {
  n_a <- nrow(a)
  n_b <- nrow(b)
  pooled_sd <- sqrt(((n_a - 1) * var(a[[pc]]) + (n_b - 1) * var(b[[pc]])) / (n_a + n_b - 2))
  (mean(a[[pc]]) - mean(b[[pc]])) / pooled_sd
}

# Do the two groups' ranges overlap at all on this axis?
ranges_overlap <- function(a, b, pc) {
  max(min(a[[pc]]), min(b[[pc]])) <= min(max(a[[pc]]), max(b[[pc]]))
}

pcs4 <- c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4")

finnish     <- subset(nordic, POP == "Finnish")
other_three <- subset(nordic, POP != "Finnish")
english     <- subset(nordic, POP == "English")
nor_ice     <- subset(nordic, POP %in% c("Norwegian", "Icelandic"))
norwegian   <- subset(nordic, POP == "Norwegian")
icelandic   <- subset(nordic, POP == "Icelandic")

cat("population means:\n")
print(round_num(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4) ~ POP, data = nordic, FUN = mean), 4),
      row.names = FALSE)

separation_pairs <- data.frame(
  PC                = pcs4,
  finn_d            = sapply(pcs4, function(pc) cohens_d(finnish, other_three, pc)),
  finn_overlap      = sapply(pcs4, function(pc) ranges_overlap(finnish, other_three, pc)),
  english_d         = sapply(pcs4, function(pc) cohens_d(english, nor_ice, pc)),
  norway_vs_iceland = sapply(pcs4, function(pc) cohens_d(norwegian, icelandic, pc))
)

cat("\nseparation on each axis (Cohen's d):\n")
print(round_num(separation_pairs, 2), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 7.3 Quantifying "separation"

The natural measure: of all the variation along a given PC, **what share lies between populations
rather than within them?** If populations are cleanly separated, most of the spread is between group
means. If the labels are meaningless on that axis, almost all the spread is within groups.

That quantity is called $\eta^2$ (eta squared), and it is a close relative of $F_{ST}$ — which you
have met as the share of genetic variation that lies between populations rather than within them.
Same idea, applied to one PC instead of to allele frequencies.

$$\eta^2 = \frac{\sum_g n_g (\bar{x}_g - \bar{x})^2}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
= \frac{\text{variation between population means}}{\text{total variation}}$$

It runs from 0 (the population labels tell you nothing about where an individual falls on this axis)
to 1 (knowing the population tells you the position exactly).

```{r eta-squared}
eta_squared <- function(df, value, group) {
  x <- df[[value]]
  g <- df[[group]]
  grand_mean <- mean(x)
  ss_total <- sum((x - grand_mean)^2)
  ss_between <- sum(tapply(x, g, function(v) length(v) * (mean(v) - grand_mean)^2))
  ss_between / ss_total
}

# how well does each PC separate the four Nordic populations?
# a formal test alongside it: does any population mean differ on this PC?
separation <- data.frame(
  PC = factor(PCS, levels = PCS),
  eta_squared = vapply(PCS, function(pc) eta_squared(nordic, pc, "POP"), numeric(1)),
  p_value = vapply(PCS, function(pc) {
    anova(aov(nordic[[pc]] ~ nordic$POP))[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
  }, numeric(1))
)

print(round(data.frame(separation[, -1], row.names = PCS), 4))
```

```{r eta-squared-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(separation, aes(PC, eta_squared, fill = p_value < 0.01)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2ca02c", "FALSE" = "grey65"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.01", "FALSE" = "not significant"),
                    name = NULL) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(y = expression(eta^2 * ": share of variation between populations"), x = NULL,
       title = "How well does each PC separate English / Norwegian / Finnish / Icelandic?")
```

# 8. Geography against genetics

## 8.1 📝 Hand-in question 6: do the ancient samples' coordinates predict their PCs?

`dataWE_LatLong.txt` gives the latitude and longitude of the site each **ancient** individual was
excavated from. If the principal components track ancestry, and ancestry varies across space, the
coordinates should correlate with the PCs.

Load it and merge it onto `dataWE` by the `IND` column.

<details>
<summary><b>💡 Hint (click to open)</b></summary>

* `read.table(file.path(data_dir, "dataWE_LatLong.txt"), sep = "\t", header = TRUE)`
* `merge(dataWE, latlong, by = "IND")` keeps only the rows present in **both** tables (an inner
  join, the default) — which is what you want, since only ancient individuals have coordinates.

</details>

```{r solved-q6}
latlong <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "dataWE_LatLong.txt"), sep = "\t", header = TRUE)
geo <- merge(dataWE, latlong, by = "IND")

cat("rows after merging:", nrow(geo), "\n")
cat("ancient individuals in dataWE:", sum(dataWE$ModAnc != "Modern"), "\n")
head(geo)
```

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal solution</b></summary>

```r
latlong <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "dataWE_LatLong.txt"), sep = "\t", header = TRUE)
geo <- merge(dataWE, latlong, by = "IND")

cat("rows after merging:", nrow(geo), "\n")
cat("ancient individuals in dataWE:", sum(dataWE$ModAnc != "Modern"), "\n")
head(geo)
```

</details>

**First observation, before any statistics:** the merge gives **191** rows but there are **220**
ancient individuals. 29 ancient individuals have no coordinates, so they drop out silently. This is
normal for ancient DNA — provenance information is not always published — but you should say so when
you report the result, because an inner join quietly changing your sample size is one of the most
common ways to mislead yourself.

```{r missing-coords}
missing_coords <- subset(dataWE, ModAnc != "Modern" & !(IND %in% latlong$IND))

cat(nrow(missing_coords), "ancient individuals without coordinates, from these populations:\n")
sort(table(missing_coords$POP), decreasing = TRUE)
```

**Plot the coordinates first.** They
are latitudes and longitudes, so you already know what they should look like: a rough map of West

### ❓ Question: What is wrong with that map?

Look at the range of the latitudes, and at the stray points.

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Reveal answer</b></summary>

Latitude runs from **10.81** to **85.45**. Both ends are impossible for this dataset:

* Latitude 10.81° N is in **Somalia / the Gulf of Aden**.
* Latitude 85.45° N is in the **Arctic Ocean**, several hundred km from the nearest land.

West Eurasian archaeological sites of the Neolithic and Bronze Age should fall roughly between 35°
and 62° N. Something is wrong with some of the rows, and plotting it took five seconds.

</details>


**Eight rows, at seven distinct sites, all with IDs starting `RISE`** (the Bronze Age samples from
Allentoft et al. 2015). And in every one of them, **latitude and longitude have been swapped.**
Swap them back and each lands exactly where its archaeological label says it should:

| Individual | `POP` | As recorded | Swapped back | Where that is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RISE175, RISE179 | Northern_LNBA | 13.60, 55.40 | 55.40 N, 13.60 E | Scania, southern Sweden ✓ |
| RISE210 | Northern_LNBA | 14.10, 56.00 | 56.00 N, 14.10 E | southern Sweden ✓ |
| RISE109, RISE150, RISE154 | Central_LNBA | ~17.0, ~51.0 | ~51.0 N, ~17.0 E | Silesia, Poland ✓ |
| RISE471 | Central_LNBA_outlier | 10.81, 48.17 | 48.17 N, 10.81 E | Bavaria, Germany ✓ |
| RISE512 | Andronovo_outlier | 85.45, 53.46 | 53.46 N, 85.45 E | Altai, Russia ✓ |

As recorded, they sit in the Gulf of Aden, the Arabian Sea and the Arctic Ocean. Swapped, they sit
in exactly the right archaeological regions. This is a real error in the data file you were given,
not something about ancient DNA.

</details>

### 📝 TODO: Fix them, then do the correlation

Make a corrected copy of `geo` with those eight rows' latitude and longitude exchanged, then compute
the correlation of `Latitude` and `Longitude` with `PC1` and `PC2` — before and after the fix, so
you can see what the error was doing to your conclusion.

<details>
<summary><b>💡 Hint (click to open)</b></summary>

```r
geo_fixed <- geo
bad <- geo$Latitude < 30 | geo$Latitude > 70
geo_fixed[bad, c("Latitude", "Longitude")] <- geo[bad, c("Longitude", "Latitude")]
```

`cor.test(x, y)` returns an object; `$estimate` is the coefficient *r* and `$p.value` the p-value.
To build the comparison table, loop over the two data frames, the two PCs and the two coordinates.

```{r solved-fix}
geo_fixed <- geo
bad <- geo$Latitude < 30 | geo$Latitude > 70
geo_fixed[bad, c("Latitude", "Longitude")] <- geo[bad, c("Longitude", "Latitude")]

correlations <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("raw", "fixed"), function(label) {
  table_in_use <- if (label == "raw") geo else geo_fixed
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PC1", "PC2"), function(pc) {
    do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Latitude", "Longitude"), function(coord) {
      test <- cor.test(table_in_use[[pc]], table_in_use[[coord]])
      data.frame(data = label, PC = pc, coordinate = coord,
                 r = round(unname(test$estimate), 3),
                 p = signif(test$p.value, 3))
    }))
  }))
}))

print(correlations, row.names = FALSE)
```

<summary><b>✅ Reveal solution</b></summary>

### ❓ Question: Report and interpret the correlations

## 8.3 Pseudo-replication: how many independent points do you really have?


```{r pseudoreplication}
cat("individuals:", nrow(geo_fixed), "\n")
cat("distinct sampling locations:",
    nrow(unique(geo_fixed[, c("Latitude", "Longitude")])), "\n")
```

191 individuals, but only **89 distinct coordinate pairs**. Several individuals share a site exactly
— they were excavated together, often from the same burial, and are frequently from the same culture
and sometimes literally related. A correlation test assumes its data points are **independent**;
these are not. The *n* that goes into the p-value is inflated, so the p-values above are too small.

A quick robustness check: collapse to one point per site (averaging the PCs of the individuals found
there) and redo the correlation with n = 89.

```{r site-level}
by_site <- aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ Latitude + Longitude, data = geo_fixed, FUN = mean)

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PC1", "PC2"), function(pc) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Latitude", "Longitude"), function(coord) {
    ind <- cor.test(geo_fixed[[pc]], geo_fixed[[coord]])
    site <- cor.test(by_site[[pc]], by_site[[coord]])
    data.frame(PC = pc, coordinate = coord,
               r_individuals = round(unname(ind$estimate), 3),
               p_individuals = signif(ind$p.value, 3),
               r_sites = round(unname(site$estimate), 3),
               p_sites = signif(site$p.value, 3))
  }))
}))

cat("n individuals =", nrow(geo_fixed), " n sites =", nrow(by_site), "\n\n")
print(comparison, row.names = FALSE)
```

### ❓ Question: Which conclusions survive?

# 9. The East Eurasian dataset

This is a **separate PCA** with its own axes, computed from modern individuals from Russia and
Siberia, with four ancient groups projected on. `PC1` here has nothing to do with `PC1` in
`dataWE.txt`.

</details>

## 9.2 Note

**The populations are very unequal, and one label is doing a lot of work.** `Siberians` is 225 of the
296 individuals — one label covering many distinct peoples across a landmass the size of Europe
(Yakuts, Evenks, Tuvinians, Nganasans, Selkups and more, in the original data). That is why its
cloud is so much more spread out than any other group's: it is not one population.

```{r ee-numbers}
cat("means:\n")
print(round_num(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2, PC3) ~ POP, data = dataEE, FUN = mean), 4))

cat("\nstandard deviations:\n")
print(round_num(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2, PC3) ~ POP, data = dataEE, FUN = sd), 4))
```

One of the four projected groups is misleadingly named. The four ancient groups are
`Russia_Bering`, `USA_Aleut`, `USA_Kuskokwim` and `Russia_Baikal`. The first three are Arctic or
sub-Arctic maritime populations — the Bering Strait coast, the Aleutian Islands and southwestern
Alaska respectively. `Russia_Baikal` is not: Lake Baikal is in continental southern Siberia, far
from the Arctic coast, and these are ancient inland Siberians.

The data agree. In PC1–PC3 space `Russia_Baikal` sits 0.026 from the `Siberians` centroid but
0.071–0.096 from each of the three Arctic groups, and all ten of its individuals fall inside the
central 95% of the Siberian cloud on all three axes. Expect it not to behave like the other three
in the plots below.

### ❓ Question: Interpret PC1 and PC2

Which populations cluster, which separate, is it what geography predicts?

Let's run the same $\eta^2$ scan as in Section 7, since we now have the tool.

```{r ee-eta, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
separation_ee <- data.frame(
  PC = factor(PCS, levels = PCS),
  eta_squared = vapply(PCS, function(pc) eta_squared(dataEE, pc, "POP"), numeric(1)),
  p_value = vapply(PCS, function(pc) {
    anova(aov(dataEE[[pc]] ~ dataEE$POP))[["Pr(>F)"]][1]
  }, numeric(1))
)

print(round(data.frame(separation_ee[, -1], row.names = PCS), 4))

ggplot(separation_ee, aes(PC, eta_squared, fill = p_value < 0.01)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2ca02c", "FALSE" = "grey65"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.01", "FALSE" = "not significant"),
                    name = NULL) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(y = expression(eta^2), x = NULL,
       title = "East Eurasian data: how well does each PC separate the 6 populations?")
```
